passages.happening: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood: Grace and peace be yours in abundance” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
The letter begins the way letters did in the ancient world: who it is from, who it is to, and a greeting. But Peter fills each part with meaning.

The sender is Peter, the fisherman whom Jesus called, who denied him three times and was restored, and who preached at Pentecost. Now he writes to believers he may never have met.

The readers are ‘exiles of the Dispersion’. ‘The Dispersion’ was the name for Jews living outside the land of Israel, and ‘exile’ recalled Israel's captivity in Babylon. Yet most of these readers were Gentiles. Peter is telling them that their sense of not belonging any more is not an accident. They have joined God's people, whose true home is elsewhere.

They lived in five Roman provinces covering much of Asia Minor, a vast area of cities, towns and farmland. How the gospel first reached some of these places, no one knows.

And they are ‘chosen’. Peter names all three persons of God at work: the Father who knew them beforehand, the Spirit who set them apart, and Jesus Christ, whose blood was sprinkled for them. This pattern, three persons working together in salvation, is what the church later confessed as the Trinity.

‘Sprinkling by His blood’ recalls the day at Sinai when Moses sprinkled the blood of the covenant on the people. It speaks of belonging to the people of God's covenant.

For people who had lost their place in their towns, these first words said: you have a place. God chose you.
passages.ot:
‘Exiles’ was Israel's word for its own people far from home. Abraham said to the Hittites, “I am a foreigner and an outsider among you” (Genesis 23:4). A psalm prays, “For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers” (Psalm 39:12).

God chose Israel out of love, not because of anything in them: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7).

The sprinkled blood recalls Sinai: “So Moses took the blood, sprinkled it on the people, and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words’” (Exodus 24:8).
passages.hard:
What does it mean to be chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father”?

Christians agree that salvation begins with God's gracious choice, not ours. They understand that choice in different ways. These notes set out the main readings and do not choose.

Reformed Christians hold that ‘foreknowledge’ here means more than knowing facts ahead of time. It is God's loving commitment to his people beforehand, the same word Peter uses of Christ in verse 20, and election is God's free choice of particular people for salvation.

Arminian and Wesleyan Christians hold that God chooses those he knows beforehand will respond in faith, and that his grace enables that response but does not force it.

Others, in both traditions, stress that election in Scripture is often of a people: God chooses a people, now those who are in Christ, as he once chose Israel, and each person comes into that people by faith.

All of these views agree that God's choice is gracious, that it gives assurance to believers under pressure, and that it leads to obedience: Peter says they were chosen ‘for obedience’. The site's Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, sets out each case.

If you are afraid that you are not chosen, hear the invitation of Jesus: “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Where do you feel like a stranger because of your faith? Ask what it would mean to hear, there, that God chose you. And ask whether being chosen has made you humble and obedient, or only comfortable.

passages.t: A living hope, and faith tested like gold
passages.happening:
Peter breaks into praise. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you, who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time” (verses 3-5).

“In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (verses 6-7).

“Though you have not seen Him, you love Him; and though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy, now that you are receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
In Greek, verses 3 to 12 are one long, flowing outpouring of praise. It begins the way Jewish prayers often began, ‘Blessed be God’, and adds the name of Christ.

‘New birth’ is a word found in the New Testament only in this letter. Salvation is God giving life, not people achieving it, as Jesus said that a person must be ‘born again’. And what they are born into is ‘a living hope’. It is living because Jesus is living. It rests on something that has happened, the resurrection, and looks to something that will happen, his revelation at the end.

Then the inheritance. The readers had lost much: friends, standing, perhaps business. Their inheritance cannot be lost. Peter piles up three words: it cannot perish, cannot be spoiled, cannot fade. It is kept for them in heaven. And they themselves are kept: ‘shielded by God’s power’, like a town under guard.

Then he speaks honestly about grief. They ‘suffer grief in various trials’. Peter does not pretend it is not painful. But he gives the grief a frame: it is ‘for a little while’, and it tests faith the way fire tests gold. Gold was refined by fire to burn off what was not gold. Faith that comes through the fire is shown to be real, and it is worth more than gold, which in the end perishes anyway.

And there is a tender line. ‘Though you have not seen Him, you love Him.’ Peter had seen Jesus with his own eyes. His readers never had. Yet they loved him and rejoiced in him. Peter honours their faith.
passages.ot:
Israel's inheritance was the land, divided among the tribes: “The land is to be divided among the tribes as an inheritance” (Numbers 26:53). The psalms already reached beyond land to God himself: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (Psalm 16:5).

The prophets spoke of God refining his people like metal: “I will refine them like silver and test them like gold. They will call on My name, and I will answer them” (Zechariah 13:9). And a psalm says, “For You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver” (Psalm 66:10).
passages.hard:
Does Peter mean that God sends suffering to test people, or that suffering is a sign that something is wrong with their faith?

Peter says trials come, and that faith can be proven and purified through them, as gold through fire. He does not say that every hardship is sent as a test, and he never says that suffering is God's punishment. He calls it grief, and he does not tell anyone to stop grieving. He sets it ‘for a little while’ against an inheritance that cannot be lost.

If you are in a hard place now, these verses do not ask you to feel comforted on demand. They tell you that God is called ‘the God of all comfort’, and that comfort often comes through people. If your trouble is heavy, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what your hope rests on: something that may be lost, or the risen Christ. Ask what trial you are in now, and what it may be proving in you. And ask whether you love the Christ you have not seen, and what that love looks like on an ordinary day.

passages.happening:
“Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully, trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (verses 10-11).

“It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Peter's readers might have felt small and late, people on the edge of the world who had only just heard. Peter tells them that the prophets of Israel, long ago, were serving them.

The prophets spoke of a grace that was coming. They did not know everything about it. They searched their own words, trying to understand the ‘time and setting’ they pointed to. Peter says that the Spirit who spoke through them was ‘the Spirit of Christ’, pointing ahead to two things: ‘the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow’. That pattern, suffering first and then glory, is the pattern of the whole letter.

What the prophets longed to see, the readers have now heard, through people who preached to them by the same Holy Spirit. And ‘even angels long to look into these things’. The word means to stoop to look, the word John uses of the disciple who stooped to look into the empty tomb (John 20:5).

So the readers are not small at all. They stand at the place in the story where heaven itself is watching.
passages.ot:
Daniel is one picture of a prophet searching the Scriptures to understand God's timing: “I, Daniel, understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years” (Daniel 9:2).

The pattern of suffering and then glory is clearest in Isaiah's servant songs. The servant will be exalted: “Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13). Yet he is also the one who “was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). Peter will quote that chapter in 2:22-25.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have thought of your faith as small and late, or as the place the prophets were looking toward. Ask what it means that suffering came before glory even for Christ. And ask what you would see if you bent down to look closely at the gospel, as the angels long to.

passages.t: Be holy, as people bought at a price
passages.happening:
“Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance. But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy’” (verses 13-16).

“Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear during your stay as foreigners. For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (verses 17-19).

“He was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake. Through Him you believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him; and so your faith and hope are in God” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
‘Therefore.’ The praise turns to commands, and each command grows from what God has done.

‘Prepare your minds for action’ is, in Greek, ‘gird up the loins of your mind’. People in long robes tucked them into their belts before running or working. Get ready, Peter says. Be clear-headed. Fix your hope on what is coming.

Then holiness. To be holy means to be set apart for God. These readers had once lived by ‘the passions of your former ignorance’. Now they belong to a holy God, and their lives are to show it. Peter quotes the command God gave Israel in Leviticus.

‘Your stay as foreigners’ uses a word for the status of resident aliens, people who lived in a place without the rights of citizens. Many in Asia Minor knew that status. Peter says it describes believers: their life here is a stay abroad, lived in ‘reverent fear’, the deep respect owed to a Father who judges fairly.

Then the reason. They were ‘redeemed’, set free by a price paid. In the Roman world silver and gold were the usual price to free a slave or a captive. Peter's readers knew it. But the price paid for them was far greater: ‘the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot’. Readers who knew the Old Testament would think of the Passover lamb, which had to be without blemish, and of Israel set free from Egypt.

And this was no afterthought. Christ ‘was known before the foundation of the world’. God's plan to rescue his people in Christ was there from the beginning.
passages.ot:
‘Be holy, because I am holy’ comes from Leviticus: “consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44), and “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2).

The Passover lamb had to be perfect: “Your lamb must be an unblemished year-old male” (Exodus 12:5). And its blood marked God's people for rescue: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13).

Isaiah had promised a redemption without money: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed” (Isaiah 52:3).
passages.asks: Ask what ‘the passions of your former ignorance’ still pull at you. Ask what it would mean to live this week as someone set apart for God. And ask whether you think of your life as bought, at the price of Christ's blood, and what that changes.

passages.happening:
“Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart. For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God” (verses 22-23).

“For, ‘All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ And this is the word that was proclaimed to you” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Peter has called them to holiness toward God. Now he calls them to love toward one another. The two belong together.

They already have ‘a genuine love’ for the other believers. Peter urges them on: love ‘deeply’, a word that means fervently, earnestly. Their old circles of friends had turned against them. Now they had a new family, and it needed real love to hold it together.

Why can they love like this? Because they have been ‘born again’, and the seed God used will not die. Ordinary seed rots away. God's word lives and lasts.

Then Peter quotes Isaiah. Human life and human glory are like grass and wildflowers: fresh in the spring, gone in a few hot days. The readers' neighbours may have seemed powerful, and their own losses heavy. But all of that fades. God's word stands. And, Peter adds, that lasting word is the very gospel they heard.
passages.ot:
Peter quotes Isaiah 40, a chapter of comfort for exiles: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). It was first spoken to God's people in exile, promising that God would bring them home. Peter speaks it to a new people of exiles.

The new birth fulfils the prophets' promise of a new heart: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
passages.asks: Ask who in your church you find hard to love deeply, and what one step toward them would look like. Ask what you are leaning on that will fade like grass. And ask whether you trust the word that stands forever.
